case_study_insert.main_stem: Riverbend Eco Stays (RES) is a cooperative in the tourism and hospitality sector, running sustainable forest eco-lodges and employing a workforce of 34. Founded in 2013 by Tariq Ndiaye, RES is member-led with a flat structure and democratic leadership, so workers share decisions on sustainability. It plans to invest $420,000 in solar-powered cabins and a recycling facility, financed by $240,000 of member share capital and a $180,000 bank loan. RES has fixed costs of $144,000 a year, a variable cost of $20.00 a unit and a selling price of $38.00, and currently produces 16,000 units a year, each unit being one guest-night. Food-waste levels have risen to 11% of purchases and guest complaints are growing, concerning the founder.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Sustainability and Guest Report — Q3 2025: RES recorded 3,900 guest-nights at $38.00 each with 85% occupancy. Food waste rose to 11% of purchases from 7% a year ago, and guest complaints climbed from 15 to 29 a month. A survey of 320 eco-tourists found 66% chose RES for its green credentials and 59% would pay $2.50 more for solar-powered cabins. Installing solar panels costs $600 per cabin. Average energy use is 18 kWh per guest-night.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Riverbend Eco Stays as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, increasing costs on RES's $180,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.40 to $14.14 per hour from April 2026, increasing the housekeeping wage bill. (3) Renewable equipment and organic food input costs have risen 8.7% year-on-year while tourism inflation is 4.9%, and eco-tourism bookings grew 5.4%.

questions.question_text: RES is funding its new solar cabins partly with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for RES of using member share capital instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The $240,000 of member share capital needs no interest or repayment, protecting cash flow while the cooperative already has fixed costs of $144,000 a year and a $180,000 loan. Money not spent on interest can fund the $600-per-cabin solar panels and cut the 11% food waste, preserving the $18.00 earned on each $38.00 guest-night.

Point 2: Member share capital is not secured on RES's assets, so the solar cabins and recycling facility cannot be repossessed if eco-tourism demand slips. As a cooperative, the 34 members also keep democratic control of sustainability decisions without a lender's conditions, and dividends can be waived in a poor year, giving flexibility while the $420,000 investment gets underway. Although member share capital means profits are shared among the cooperative, it avoids the extra interest that the 0.75-point rise to 4.5% would add on a $180,000 loan, leaving more of the $18.00 contribution for the 34 members. It also fits the democratic culture Tariq Ndiaye established at the eco-lodges.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to RES, its member share capital and its eco-lodges.

questions.question_text: RES is promoting its new solar-powered cabins. Consider a national radio campaign, an eco-travel magazine advert, or social media influencer marketing. Which should RES choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National radio campaign: Radio can reach many listeners quickly across a wide region and suits a simple message about the new solar-powered cabins. Yet airtime is costly for a cooperative spending $420,000, and many listeners live too far from the forest lodges to book a $38.00 guest-night, so much of the spend would not convert.

Eco-travel magazine advert: A specialist magazine targets exactly the 66% of surveyed eco-tourists who chose RES for its green credentials and the 59% who would pay $2.50 more for solar cabins. It is credible and on-message, but print has a limited circulation, long lead times and no immediate booking route, so it may not fill rooms fast enough to justify the new build.

Social media influencer marketing: Sustainability and travel influencers can demonstrate the solar cabins and recycling facility to the same 320-person survey audience, with measurable engagement and low cost per lead. Results take time and depend on credible creators, but content can carry the green message powerfully.

Recommendation: RES should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the eco-conscious segment in the research, is far cheaper than national radio and more immediate than print, and it showcases the $420,000 investment to exactly those who would pay the $2.50 premium. Radio is rejected as wasteful and untargeted; the magazine is rejected as slow and narrow, though it could support the campaign later. With only 34 staff, the cooperative cannot fund a costly national campaign, and a low-cost digital approach fits its member-led culture. Influencers can also explain the $600-per-cabin solar panels and the recycling facility to the 320 surveyed eco-tourists more personally than print.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of RES with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of RES with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and the magazine are rejected.

questions.question_text: Food waste at RES has risen to 11% of purchases. Explain two benefits for RES of using team working to tackle this problem.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working brings the 34 members together to share ideas on portion control and recycling, which suits the cooperative's democratic culture and can cut the 11% food waste figure back toward 7%. Joint problem-solving uses the knowledge of lodge staff closest to the kitchen, lowering the $20.00 variable cost per guest-night and protecting the $18.00 contribution on each $38.00 booking.

Point 2: Working in teams raises motivation and shared responsibility, helping reduce the 29 monthly guest complaints because everyone owns service quality. Stronger team spirit also supports the flat structure and cuts the risk of staff leaving, so the $600-per-cabin solar installation and the wider $420,000 investment are delivered by a stable, committed workforce. Reducing waste from 11% toward 7% would lower the $20.00 variable cost and lift the $18.00 contribution across all 16,000 guest-nights. Team working also suits the cooperative's democratic leadership and gives the 34 members a shared stake in cutting the 29 monthly complaints.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RES's waste, complaints and cooperative structure.

questions.question_text: RES wants staff to cut the 11% food waste. Consider financial motivators such as a bonus or non-financial motivators such as job enrichment. Which should RES choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Financial motivators (bonus): Linking a bonus to lower food waste gives the 34 members a direct cash incentive to reduce the 11% figure toward 7%, which would cut the $20.00 variable cost per guest-night and lift the $18.00 contribution. It is easy to measure against the report, but bonuses add to the wage bill, can encourage short-term corner-cutting on the 85% occupancy service, and may breed competition rather than the cooperative's team spirit.

Non-financial motivators (job enrichment): Giving staff responsibility for sustainability targets and the recycling facility makes the work more meaningful, fitting RES's green credentials that 66% of eco-tourists value. It can raise commitment and reduce the 29 monthly complaints at little cash cost, but results are slower and depend on staff wanting more responsibility; without any reward, some members may not respond.

Decision: RES should choose job enrichment, supported by a small team-based bonus. Job enrichment fits the cooperative's democratic culture, costs little while $420,000 is committed and addresses waste and complaints together. A large individual bonus scheme is rejected because it adds cost, risks undermining teamwork and may not tackle the root causes of waste; modest recognition can be added later. A bonus must be affordable against fixed costs of $144,000 and the $180,000 loan, so job enrichment gives a lower-cost first step for the 34 members. If the $600 solar-cabin programme and the recycling facility raise pride in the brand, non-financial rewards may tackle waste more durably. Small team recognition for waste targets can be added later without the cost of a full bonus scheme.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivator approaches with limited application to RES.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both approaches in the context of RES.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of RES with a well-justified decision covering cost, culture and effectiveness.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RES's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $144,000 ÷ ($38.00 − $20.00) = $144,000 ÷ $18.00 = 8,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 8,000 guest-night units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $38.00 − $20.00 = $18.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $18.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RES's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 8,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 16,000 guest-nights to confirm the lodges are profitable, leaving a margin of safety of 8,000 guest-nights.
2. Contribution per unit of $18.00 lets RES model the $2.50 premium that 59% of eco-tourists would pay for solar cabins, showing how the $420,000 investment could be recovered through higher contribution.
3. The break-even figure helps plan interest on the $180,000 loan and returns to the $240,000 member share capital, checking that 16,000 guest-nights cover fixed costs of $144,000 before more borrowing.
4. Average total cost of $29.00 a unit ($144,000 ÷ 16,000 + $20.00) can be benchmarked against 85% occupancy and the 11% food-waste rate, guiding the $600-per-cabin spending as renewable input costs rise 8.7%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 8,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $18.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 16,000 guest-nights; modelling the $2.50 solar premium; loan and member-capital planning for the $420,000 investment; and average total cost benchmarking at $29.00 to tackle waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RES's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has RES's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.28 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.62 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.84 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.15 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $55,000 inventories + $85,000 trade receivables + $20,000 cash = $160,000; 2025 current assets = $60,000 + $105,000 + $45,000 = $210,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 = $160,000 ÷ $125,000 = 1.28 and 2025 = $210,000 ÷ $130,000 = 1.62. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($160,000 − $55,000) ÷ $125,000 = 0.84 and 2025 = ($210,000 − $60,000) ÷ $130,000 = 1.15.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. The 2024 figure of 1.28 rose to 1.62 as cash more than doubled from $20,000 to $45,000 while current liabilities rose only slightly from $125,000 to $130,000. The stricter measure, which removes inventories, improved from 0.84 to 1.15, so RES can now meet short-term debts without selling stock — valuable while it services a $180,000 loan and funds $420,000 of solar cabins. However, trade receivables grew from $85,000 to $105,000, tying up cash, so credit control still matters.

Conclusion: RES's financial position has improved. Both measures rose (1.28 to 1.62 and 0.84 to 1.15) and the cash increase makes the improvement genuine rather than stock-driven. The remaining risk is higher receivables, so RES should chase these while proceeding with the eco-cabin investment. The improved $45,000 cash balance also helps absorb the 8.7% input inflation without delaying the $420,000 solar-cabin programme. Collecting the $105,000 of receivables promptly will keep the upward trend in both measures intact next year.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether RES's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RES of installing solar panels on its cabins.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Solar power cuts reliance on bought energy, helping offset the 8.7% rise in renewable equipment and organic input costs and reducing the $20.00 variable cost per guest-night. The 59% of surveyed eco-tourists who would pay $2.50 more for solar cabins support the $38.00 price, while 18 kWh per guest-night shows where savings can be made, strengthening the $420,000 investment's returns.

Disadvantage: Panels cost $600 per cabin, adding to fixed costs of $144,000 a year at a time when RES has a $180,000 loan and is spending $420,000. If 85% occupancy falls, payback is slower, and installation disruption could worsen the 29 monthly complaints and the 11% waste problem before the benefits arrive. Without the $2.50 premium, the $600-per-cabin cost would take longer to recover if 85% occupancy softens. The panels must also deliver the energy savings implied by the 18 kWh figure, otherwise the $20.00 variable cost will not fall as hoped.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RES's survey, costs and sustainability goals.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in renewable and organic input costs will affect RES. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If RES's $180,000 loan is variable-rate, annual interest rises by 0.75% of $180,000 = $1,350. That is small against fixed costs of $144,000, and if the loan is fixed the direct cost is nil. Higher rates could still slow eco-tourism spending, but RES can limit the risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $14.14 per hour): With a workforce of 34, many housekeeping and lodge roles are hourly-paid, so the rise feeds into the wage bill. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the sound comparison is the given output of 16,000 guest-nights across 34 staff, about 471 guest-nights per worker. If productivity holds and waste falls from 11%, the $18.00 contribution can absorb it; if complaints keep rising, unit labour cost grows.

Input cost inflation (8.7%): The $20.00 variable cost per unit is where renewable equipment and organic food sit, but the insert gives no breakdown, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $20.00 rose 8.7%, that is 0.087 × $20.00 = $1.74 per unit, about $27,840 a year at 16,000 guest-nights. Even a $1.50-per-unit rise costs $24,000 a year, cutting contribution from $18.00 toward $16.50.

Conclusion: The 8.7% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact because it recurs on all 16,000 guest-nights and erodes the $18.00 contribution that supports the $420,000 solar-cabin project. The wage rise matters but is manageable if productivity holds, while the interest rise adds only about $1,350.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to RES.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on RES's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of RES with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
